{{< include latex-macros/macros.qmd >}}

In an **observational study**,
treatment is not assigned by the investigator.
Instead, individuals self-select into treatment,
or treatment is assigned based on clinical or administrative criteria.
As a result, treatment groups may differ systematically
in ways that also affect the [outcome](Intro-to-GLMs.qmd#def-outcome) —
this systematic difference is called **[confounding](#def-confounding-obs)**.

## Confounding {#sec-causal-confounding}

<!-- No slidebreak here: the heading shares its slide with the def-confounding-obs div. -->
:::{#def-confounding-obs}
#### Confounding

**Confounding** occurs when there is a common cause
of both the treatment $A$ and the outcome $Y$.
This common cause is called a **[confounder](#def-confounder)**.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-confounding-potential-outcomes}
#### Confounding in the potential outcomes framework

In the [potential outcomes](#def-potential-outcomes) framework,
confounding means that treatment assignment is not [independent](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/independence.html#def-indpt)
of potential outcomes:
$$A \not\perp\!\!\!\perp (Y(0), Y(1))$$

As a result, the observed association between $A$ and $Y$
does not equal the causal effect of $A$ on $Y$.
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-confounding-coffee}
#### Confounding of coffee and lung cancer by smoking

Consider a hypothetical cohort of 1000 adults,
with coffee drinking $A$ ($A = 1$ for daily coffee),
lung cancer $Y$ ($Y = 1$ for diagnosis during follow-up),
and smoking $L$ ($L = 1$ for smokers).
Suppose coffee has **no** effect on lung cancer,
so that $Y_i(1) = Y_i(0)$ for every individual,
but smokers are both more likely to drink coffee
and more likely to develop lung cancer:

| $L$ | coffee | no coffee | $\Pf{Y = 1 \mid A = 1, L}$ | $\Pf{Y = 1 \mid A = 0, L}$ |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| 0 (nonsmokers) | 200 | 500 | 0.01 | 0.01 |
| 1 (smokers) | 200 | 100 | 0.10 | 0.10 |

Within each smoking stratum,
the risk difference is $0$,
matching the true (null) causal effect.
Ignoring smoking:

$$
\ba
\Pf{Y = 1 \mid A = 1}
&= \frac{200 \cdot 0.01 + 200 \cdot 0.10}{400}
&& \text{(average over the 400 coffee drinkers)} \\
&= \frac{2 + 20}{400}
&& \text{(multiply)} \\
&= \frac{22}{400}
&& \text{(add)} \\
&= 0.055
&& \text{(divide)} \\
\Pf{Y = 1 \mid A = 0}
&= \frac{500 \cdot 0.01 + 100 \cdot 0.10}{600}
&& \text{(average over the 600 non-drinkers)} \\
&= \frac{5 + 10}{600}
&& \text{(multiply)} \\
&= \frac{15}{600}
&& \text{(add)} \\
&= 0.025
&& \text{(divide)} \\
\Pf{Y = 1 \mid A = 1} - \Pf{Y = 1 \mid A = 0}
&= 0.055 - 0.025
&& \text{(subtract the two crude risks)} \\
&= 0.03
&& \text{(subtract)}
\ea
$$

The crude risk difference of $0.03$ suggests that coffee is harmful,
even though coffee has no effect in this cohort.
Because $Y_i(0) = Y_i(1) = Y_i$ for everyone here,
the crude risks are also the mean [potential outcomes](#def-potential-outcomes) under no coffee in each group:
$\E{Y(0) \mid A = 1} = 0.055 \neq 0.025 = \E{Y(0) \mid A = 0}$.
So $A \not\ind Y(0)$,
which is the failure of unconditional exchangeability
described in @rem-confounding-potential-outcomes.
Smoking $L$ is a [confounder](#def-confounder):
it is a common cause of $A$ and $Y$.

:::

## Why observational studies are harder than randomized trials {#sec-causal-obs-harder}

In a [randomized experiment](#sec-causal-rct),
the investigator controls treatment assignment,
so the identification assumptions hold by design
[@hernan2020causal, Chapter 3]:

- randomization makes the groups [exchangeable](#def-exchangeability)
  without conditioning on any covariates (@def-unconditional-exchangeability);
- the randomization probabilities are strictly between 0 and 1,
  so [positivity](#def-positivity) holds;
- the protocol specifies the treatment,
  which supports [consistency](#def-consistency).

In an observational study,
none of these assumptions is guaranteed by design
[@hernan2020causal, Chapter 3]:

- exchangeability (@def-exchangeability) can hold at best conditionally on measured covariates $\vec{L}$,
  so we must measure and adjust for a sufficient set of confounders,
  and we cannot check from the data that no confounder is missing;
- positivity (@def-positivity) can fail
  when some covariate patterns, such as the most severe patients, are always (or never) treated;
- consistency (@def-consistency) requires a well-defined treatment,
  which is harder to ensure when "treatment" is a self-chosen exposure,
  such as "drinks coffee" in @exm-confounding-coffee,
  that people can take up in many different ways.

[Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs)](#sec-pred-sel-dag)
help with the first of these difficulties,
by showing which covariates must be in $\vec{L}$.
More generally, DAGs provide a formal graphical tool
for representing causal assumptions
and identifying [confounders](#def-confounder), [mediators](#def-mediator), [colliders](#def-collider),
and sufficient adjustment sets.
